extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and judging lyrical/romantic poetry (as in Wordsworth/Coleridge): choosing subjects, diction, and poetic aims to produce emotional effect and novelty. Emphasises two classes of poem (supernatural/romantic vs. ordinary life) and the right language/style for each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excite sympathy by faithful adherence to truth of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of exciting the sympathy of the reader by a faithful adherence to the truth of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to move the reader's affections by representing human feelings and situations truthfully — sympathy arises from fidelity to nature rather than artificial ornament. This is presented as one of the two 'cardinal points' of poetry in the authors' practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give interest of novelty by imaginative colouring
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of giving the interest of novelty by the modifying colours of imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imagination to cast familiar things in a new light (likened to 'accidents of light and shade' such as moonlight or sunset). Novelty should complement truth of nature to create a sudden charm; the combination of both is a key poetic aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose two complementary sorts of poems (supernatural/romantic vs. ordinary life)
rubrics_metrics.description: One class: incidents and agents partly supernatural/romantic, aiming to interest the affections by the sympathetic faith of such emotions; The other class: subjects chosen from ordinary life with characters and incidents found in every village and vicinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For supernatural/romantic poems, transfer human interest and a semblance of truth sufficient to procure 'that willing suspension of disbelief' (poetic faith). For ordinary-life poems, choose humble, everyday subjects and awaken feeling by attention and truthful depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the 'language of real life' where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Fit to metrical arrangement a selection of the real language of men in a state of vivid sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wordsworth proposed managing certain subjects in the language of ordinary life (the 'language of real life') to produce pleasurable interest. This involves using ordinary, colloquial speech (not overly ornamented or extra-colloquial phrasing) when it suits the subject. The text notes controversy over extending this style universally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procure poetic faith (willing suspension of disbelief)
rubrics_metrics.description: For supernatural or romantic subjects, obtain 'that willing suspension of disbelief for the moment, which constitutes poetic faith.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make supernatural agents or incidents effective, the poet must create a human interest and enough semblance of truth that readers temporarily accept the extraordinary. This is necessary to move the reader emotionally in such poems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match diction/style to subject — reject inappropriate ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects which reject the usual ornaments and extra-colloquial style of poems may be managed in ordinary language to produce pleasure; conversely, avoid forcing the 'language of real life' where it's inconsistent with other poetic aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose diction that is appropriate to the subject matter: humble subjects suit plain, real-language diction; other subjects may call for loftier diction. The author warns against dogmatically extending one register to all poetry and stresses internal consistency between preface/theory and actual poetic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select ordinary subjects to awaken the mind's attention to overlooked loveliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose subjects from ordinary life so as to 'excite a feeling analogous to the supernatural, by awakening the mind's attention to the lethargy of custom, and directing it to the loveliness and wonders of the world before us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic effect can be achieved by making readers notice and feel the beauty in everyday scenes and people — an objective of Wordsworth's contributions to Lyrical Ballads. The poet's task includes reviving perception (eyes that see not, ears that hear not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance originality and intelligibility for public reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty is delightful when it is understood at once; when the poet presents a 'new world' that readers cannot immediately comprehend, the work risks being rejected or misunderstood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider your audience's capacity to grasp novelty: immediate comprehension makes novelty pleasurable; too unfamiliar a presentation may provoke ridicule or failure to be appreciated. Periodical critics often mirror public taste and may be slow to accept essential novelty — therefore reception depends partly on how accessible the novelty is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's proper aim: imparting pleasurable interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The peculiar business of poetry is to impart pleasurable interest (by fitting real language to metrical arrangement and by truthful, affecting depiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or composing poetry, evaluate whether the poem succeeds in producing the kind and quantity of pleasure a poet reasonably seeks to impart — whether by sympathy, novelty, or the manner of language and subject treatment.
